📉 The dashboard: The S&P 500 closed down 4.4%, as the AI trade unraveled. (See below.👇)

🥶 Today's stock spotlight: SpaceX (-9.1%) and Tesla (-10.8%) extended their declines from yesterday, as Elon Musk's companies face growing concerns about regulatory hurdles for AI data center construction and a potential merger following Democrats' election sweep.
 
 
1 big thing: AI free fall
By Matt Phillips
 
Data: Financial Modeling Prep; Chart: Pete Gannon/Axios

Tech stocks plunged today, reflecting investors' growing fears of a slowdown in the AI boom.

📉 The latest: The tech-heavy Nasdaq Composite index closed down 5.5%, firmly in correction territory, down almost 12% from its high on Oct. 6.

  • The S&P 500 wasn't far behind today, shedding 4.4%.
  • The sell-off is the stock market's worst showing since the April 2025 tariff panic.

🤖 The big picture: It comes two days after Democrats notched historic gains in the midterm elections, including taking the governorships of Texas and Ohio — areas of intense data center development.

  • In Texas, Gov.-elect Gina Hinojosa promised to impose a moratorium on new buildouts until lawmakers enact stronger protections.
  • In Ohio, Amy Acton called for conditional pauses requiring developers to cover their utility costs, provide community benefits and use union labor.

Between the lines: Their victories signal growing political resistance to arguably the largest investment boom in U.S. history.

🔍 Zoom in: AI-related shares led today's sell-off, with companies closely tied to the data center build-out posting double-digit losses.

  • Semiconductor shares plummeted, dragging the Philadelphia Semiconductor Index down over 12%. The index is now down more than 38% from its June high.
  • So-called neoclouds — companies that build data centers in order to lease out their computing power to larger players like hyperscalers — were particularly hard hit. CoreWeave, for example, was down 9.8%.
  • Even the Big Tech hyperscalers that supported the indexes with gains a day ago — Microsoft (-3.6%), Alphabet (-1.9%) and Amazon (-2.2%) — were caught in today's market downdraft.
 
 
2. 🚦Blue wave, yellow light
 

Illustration: Maura Losch/Axios
 

Tuesday's Democratic election sweep could tap the brakes on the autonomous vehicle industry's ambitious growth plans, Axios mobility expert Joann Muller writes.

  • 🗣️ The industry's hopes for federal legislation overriding state and local rules "just became a pipe dream," said Rob Grant, AV policy expert and co-founder of Autnmy AI.

🏛️ The big picture: Congress has tried and failed for nearly a decade to establish national rules for autonomous vehicles.

  • Although early bills attracted bipartisan support, Democrats lately have opposed industry-backed proposals, citing concerns about safety, labor protections and whether federal regulations should override state laws.

If Congress can't pass an AV bill, that will put more stress on state-level policy debates, notes MIT research scientist and mobility expert Bryan Reimer.

  • And AV and robotaxi companies were already running into policy roadblocks in several Democratic-led states, including New York, Illinois, Oregon and Massachusetts.

4. 🕔 After hours: Hackers turn up the heat
 

Illustration: Aïda Amer/Axios. Stock: Getty Images
 

U.S. officials warned anyone with an industrial fridge to watch out for hackers looking to turn up the heat, Axios' Pete Gannon writes.

Why it matters: A series of strange incidents — spanning European supermarket fridges, U.S. military food freezers and French blood banks — have ruined inventories and triggered small fires.

😈 Driving the news: Today, the FBI, the Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency, and the departments of Health, Transportation and Agriculture issued a joint statement warning organizations of an ongoing cyber threat "activity targeting industrial refrigeration and cold chain monitoring systems."

  • They're recommending organizations remove control systems from the internet, strengthen passwords and ensure devices are updated.
  • 🗣️ "Every organization that depends on refrigeration and monitoring systems should assume it could be a target," said Chris Butera, CISA's acting executive assistant director for cybersecurity. "We urge you to review the joint fact sheet and take action now to close known security gaps."

🗓️ On this day in 1895, patent attorney George Selden was granted the first U.S. patent for an automobile, the payoff of 16 years of patent hijinks. Selden, who never manufactured a car, repeatedly filed amendments to delay the clock on his patent, hoping to cash in on royalties once automakers caught up. For a while it worked. Then Henry Ford refused to pay, and after years in court, Selden's scheme came to a screeching halt.
